name: Sea Green
lede: Sea green is a medium bluish green with a long life in English: a color of the sea, of emeralds and of dye vats, fixed on screens by the X11 web list as #2E8B57.

sections.title: One name, several greens
sections.body:
Sea green has meant different greens to different writers. Paterson's dictionary defines it as a clear bluish green and, a few columns later, glaucous as a dull greenish blue usually descriptive of the sea; elsewhere it lists sea green as a yellowish green, and notes that it is a color in the Ostwald circle [1]. Books disagree here, and the disagreement is real: the word names a zone between blue and green, not a point [1].

Our library holds four versions. The swatch on this page is the CSS and X11 color *SeaGreen*, hex #2E8B57, one of the 140 named colors of the web list [1][2]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XIX shows a bluer, more teal-leaning tone, about #388783 in our scan of an aged plate, and the xkcd survey puts the name at a much brighter mint-like #53FCA1 [2]. Maerz and Paul date the English name to 1598 [2]. The web version is therefore the darkest and the most neutral of them, a green with a hint of blue rather than a blue with a hint of green.

sections.title: Where it sits on the color circle
sections.body:
Sea green appears early in attempts to arrange color. In his Cambridge lectures of 1669 and 1670, by Gage's account, Newton listed eleven steps of the spectrum, among them green, grass green, sea green and blue, before reducing them to seven [3]. In the 1780s the Berlin painter Johann Christoph Frisch drew an eight-part circle with sea green and leaf green as the two steps between blue and yellow [3].

In 1772 the entomologist Ignaz Schiffermuller printed a twelve-part circle in Vienna that was one of the first to set complementary colors opposite each other, and in it red faces sea green [4]. The pairing is not a coincidence of taste. Stare at red and then look at a white wall, and what you see is a pale bluish green; Goethe described a girl's red dress turning, in the after-image, into a dress of beautiful sea green [5][6][7].

Whether red's true opposite is sea green depends on the system. The painter's wheel, the light mixture and the perceptual space give different answers, so the pairing is a convention of one tradition, not a law [3][4].

sections.title: Sea green as a stage in the vat
sections.body:
The name also marks a step in dyeing. A woad or indigo vat gives wool that comes out yellowish green, and as the air reaches it, it turns sea green and then settles into blue [8]. Visitors at Merton Abbey saw skeins of wool emerge from the woad vat an almost grassy color, then deep sea green, then a resonant blue, according to St Clair [9].

The shellfish purple has a similar sequence. St Clair describes the gland fluid turning, in sunlight, from pale yellow to sea green to blue and finally to a dark purple red [10]. William Cole recorded the same changes on the shores of the Bristol Channel in 1685, in a passage that Finlay quotes: first light green, then a deep green, then dull sea green, then a blue, then purplish red [11]. Sea green in these accounts is a point on the way to somewhere else, a color you see for a moment, which fits a hue that sits between blue and green.

sections.title: Stones and minerals
sections.body:
Gem writers use the name for the green of a stone. Pliny's description of an opal, as Finlay translates it, gives it the sea green of emeralds alongside the fire of rubies and the purple of amethysts [12]. Paterson defines beryl as a pale sea green or greenish blue, the color of the stone [1]. Ball notes that chromium makes ruby deep red but emerald green, because the crystal field is stronger in emerald, and that nickel salts take a sea green [13].

The pottery green *celadon* is a cousin. The mineral celadonite was named by Glocker in 1847 from the French *céladon*, meaning sea green, after its common color [14]. It is a main component of green earth, which painters have used as a pigment [14]. Our own [[celadon]] page is paler and greyer; the stone and the glaze are a different color from the one on this swatch.

sections.title: The sea itself
sections.body:
The sea is rarely the color that bears its name. Pastoureau notes that medieval illuminators and Renaissance painters gave it a very broad palette, and that only in the modern period did painters reduce it to three dominant colors: green, grey and blue [15]. Monet's *The Green Wave* of 1866 to 1867, which Pastoureau uses as an example, is a dark saturated green and a violent image, unlike the sea his Impressionist friends painted later [15].

Green pigments were the weak point of European painting for centuries [15]. Plant greens held up badly, earth greens covered poorly, copper greens were corrosive and toxic, and Prussian-blue greens tended to fade; artificial ultramarine greens, perfected around 1825 to 1830, found a place on painters' palettes only in the 1880s [15]. A sea-green swatch in an old painting is therefore often what is left of a mixture that has moved.

sections.title: A parable and some trousers
sections.body:
Sea green turns up in a Buddhist parable [16][17]. A deity tells a boy he can have everything he wants if he can close his eyes and not think of the color sea green; the sea keeps coming back [16][17]. Finlay heard the story from a monk in Ladakh, and in his version the old man at last succeeds and smiles, realizing he already has everything he wants [16]. St Clair gives the story two endings, one ending in enlightenment and the other in madness, and calls it a fable [17]. It is a story, not a finding about perception.

Ball adds a smaller detail. Peter Griess, the chemist who found the diazo dyes, once turned up at the college in a reddish-brown overcoat, a red muffler and sea-green trousers, and the porter refused him entry; Ball notes the outfit was scarcely a sign of a soul attuned to color chemistry [18]. The anecdote is told for its comedy, and the books do not confirm that the trousers were this exact hue.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, sea green appears in only 11 paintings by area (0.05 per cent) and in 8 by the within-painting lens, as photographed, so it is rarer than 70 per cent of the named colors [19]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 6 of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 5.6 times the museums' baseline [19].

The earliest match is a painting of 1860, with a third-earliest of 1890 and a latest of 1918, in ten dated paintings [19]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike and not a pigment test. The printed word peaks in the 1800s and rose fastest in the 1890s in Google Books, which counts every use of the phrase, including the sea and the stone [19].
